headline: A Terminal Becomes the Bus for Two Rival AI Agents
lede: A developer called @shawn_pana built a small tool, *smux*, that lets Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex coordinate on tasks without any shared API, SDK, or purpose-built protocol. The only connective tissue is a terminal session. The implication is modest in scope but pointed in principle: the shell prompt may be the lowest-common-denominator interface that lets heterogeneous AI agents interoperate without anyone agreeing on a standard first.
body:
Both Claude Code and Codex are *agentic coding assistants* — programs that don't just suggest code but can read a repository, execute commands, edit files, and iterate toward a stated goal without step-by-step human direction. They run inside a terminal, and that is precisely the surface smux exploits. Rather than routing messages through a purpose-built orchestration layer, smux lets each agent create, read from, and write to terminal panes, turning the shell into a shared blackboard.

The architectural bet is that **the terminal is already a universal interface** that any sufficiently capable coding agent can operate. A human developer writes to a terminal and reads its output; so does Claude Code; so does Codex. If a tool can mediate that surface — multiplexing panes, routing output, letting one agent observe what another wrote — then inter-agent communication falls out almost for free, without either vendor shipping a joint spec.

This matters because multi-agent coordination is currently one of the harder unsolved problems in applied AI. Most frameworks that tackle it — LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen — require agents to share a runtime or speak a common protocol, which implicitly ties you to one vendor or one model family. A terminal-mediated approach sidesteps that entirely: Claude Code and Codex remain fully independent processes; smux just lets them share a workspace.

The research sources confirm that Claude Code and Codex take meaningfully different approaches even within the same terminal paradigm — Claude Code centers on a unified agent loop tightly coupled to Anthropic's model stack, while Codex (OpenAI's rebooted terminal agent, distinct from the original 2021 code-generation model of the same name) has its own architecture. That the two can be made to collaborate through a thin terminal-multiplexer layer, rather than a fat orchestration framework, is the interesting finding here.

The demo is early, and the OCR of the attached screenshot is largely illegible, so the exact interaction shown — what task the agents divided, who reviewed whose work — cannot be independently verified from the available sources. Still, the concept is clean enough to stand on its own: if the terminal is the universal substrate, a tool that treats it as a message bus could outlast any particular agent or model.

concepts.definition: Software that splits a single terminal session into multiple independent panes or windows, each running its own process. Classic examples are tmux and screen. Here, smux extends the idea so that programs — not just humans — can programmatically create panes and read their output.

An AI tool that goes beyond autocomplete or chat to autonomously read files, run shell commands, edit code, and iterate toward a goal. Claude Code and Codex are both in this category. The 'agentic' label distinguishes them from passive suggestion tools: they take actions, observe outcomes, and adjust.

The ability for two or more AI agents to exchange information and coordinate work without direct human mediation at each step. Achieving this across agents from different vendors is non-trivial because there is no agreed protocol; most solutions require a shared runtime or orchestration layer.

A classic pattern in multi-agent systems where agents coordinate by reading from and writing to a common data structure rather than sending messages directly to each other. Using a terminal as a blackboard is an informal application of this idea.

fact_check: The post refers to 'Codex' as an OpenAI product comparable to Claude Code. This warrants a note: OpenAI's original Codex was a code-generation model released in 2021 and later deprecated. The Codex referenced here is OpenAI's subsequently relaunched terminal coding agent, a distinct product. The two share a name but are architecturally different. The post's claim that communication requires 'no APIs' is accurate in the sense that no inter-agent API is needed, though both agents still rely on their respective model APIs internally.
